slides.title: The Fall of the Republic
body: The assassination of Julius Caesar on the Ides of March was the spark that toppled the fragile balance of the late Republic. In the Senate house, a conspiracy of senators who feared his accumulating power fired the act that would echo through the age.

The political landscape of the first century BCE was defined by personal armies loyal to generals rather than the state. When ambition outran institution, the machinery of the Republic began to fail with terrifying momentum.
By 27 BCE, Octavian had emerged from the civil wars as Augustus, the first citizen — princeps — cloaking monarchy in republican forms and inaugurating two centuries of imperial peace.

note.title: Scholar's Note
note.text: Augustus never used the title 'king'. His genius lay in preserving the appearance of the Republic while holding its substance.

sections.heading: Standard Equipment
sections.body: The Scutum (shield), Pilum (javelin), and Gladius (short sword) formed a lethal trinity of defensive and offensive capability.

sections.heading: Rigorous Training
sections.body: Recruits were trained to march 20 Roman miles in 5 hours carrying 60 lbs of gear, ensuring logistical superiority.

note.text: The Romans owed their conquest of the world to no other cause than military training, discipline and army organisation.

slides.title: The Silk Road Trade
slides.subtitle: Explore the intricate network of land and maritime routes that connected the Roman Empire with the wealth of the Han Dynasty and beyond.

footnotes.title: Silk & Textiles
footnotes.body: Luxury fabrics from the East, coveted by Roman elites as markers of status.

footnotes.title: Spices & Incense
footnotes.body: Cinnamon, pepper, and frankincense for culinary, medicinal, and ritual use.

footnotes.title: Grain & Glass
footnotes.body: Roman exports — glass vessels, wine, and olive oil — sent eastward in return.

note.quote: The Silk Road was not a single path, but a shifting network of desert caravans and monsoon-driven ships that reshaped the ancient world's economy.

slides.title: The Colosseum: Engineering Marvel
slides.body: To protect the 50,000+ spectators from the scorching Roman sun, engineers installed the Velarium — a massive retractable awning made of canvas, operated by a detachment of sailors from the Roman Navy using complex ropes and pulleys anchored to 240 exterior masts.

slides.title: Knowledge Check: Architecture
slides.question: Which architectural element allowed the Romans to build massive structures like the Aqueducts?

feedback.correctText: The arch let Romans redistribute compressive load outward and downward, spanning great distances with stone and concrete.
feedback.incorrectText: Consider which element redistributes weight to span gaps — think about the shape that carries load along its curve. Try again.
